lessons.title: Large Numbers to 1,000,000
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Numbers can be very large! A million is 1,000,000. Our place value system extends: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands, millions. Each place is 10 times bigger than the one to its right. Population of a city might be 3,456,789 — three million, four hundred and fifty-six thousand, seven hundred and eighty-nine.

Round population figures
Read large numbers from newspaper headlines

exercises.q: What is the value of 4 in 4,567,000?

homework.task: Find 5 large numbers in the news. Write in words and round to nearest 1000.

revision.notes: Place value extends: M, HTh, TTh, Th, H, T, O. Round: look at next digit — 5+ rounds up.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Multiplication: 2-digit × 2-digit
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Long multiplication: 34 × 26. Step 1: 34 × 6 = 204. Step 2: 34 × 20 = 680. Step 3: Add: 204 + 680 = 884. Always estimate first: 34×26 ≈ 30×30 = 900. Our answer 884 is close to 900, so it's reasonable!
practical_activities: Grid method for 2-digit multiplication
Word problems requiring multiplication
Multiplication in area calculations

revision.notes: Long multiplication: split into tens and ones. Add partial products. Estimate to check.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Fractions: Mixed Numbers and Improper
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions
lessons.reading_material: A MIXED NUMBER has a whole number and a fraction: 2 3/4. An IMPROPER FRACTION has a numerator bigger than denominator: 11/4. Converting: 2 3/4 → (2×4+3)/4 = 11/4. And back: 11÷4=2 remainder 3, so 2 3/4. We can add mixed numbers by adding whole parts and fraction parts separately.
practical_activities: Pizza model for mixed numbers
Number line with mixed fractions
Convert and add mixed number cards

homework.task: Convert these to mixed numbers: 17/5, 23/6, 31/8. Convert these to improper: 3 2/5, 4 3/7.

revision.notes: Mixed to improper: (whole × denom + num) / denom. Improper to mixed: divide, remainder becomes numerator.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Geometry: Angles
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: An ANGLE is formed when two lines meet at a point. RIGHT ANGLE = 90° (like a corner of a square). ACUTE ANGLE < 90° (sharp angle). OBTUSE ANGLE is between 90° and 180°. STRAIGHT ANGLE = 180° (a straight line). A protractor measures angles in degrees. Triangles can be classified: right-angled (has 90°), acute (all angles <90°), obtuse (one angle >90°).
practical_activities: Angle hunt around the school
Measure angles with protractors
Create angle art with rulers

homework.task: Draw and label examples of acute, right, and obtuse angles. Measure each one.

revision.notes: Right=90°, Acute<90°, Obtuse 90-180°, Straight=180°. Sum of triangle angles = 180°.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Grammar: Tenses
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Use simple past, present, and future tenses
lessons.reading_material: TENSE tells us when an action happens. PAST TENSE: happened before now (walked, ran, said). PRESENT TENSE: happening now (walk, run, say/walks, runs, says). FUTURE TENSE: will happen later (will walk, will run, will say). Irregular verbs don't follow the -ed pattern: go→went, eat→ate, see→saw. Good writers stay in one tense throughout a piece!
practical_activities: Tense timeline activity
Spot the tense error in paragraphs
Retell a story in past tense

exercises.q: Correct: 'Yesterday I go to the park'
exercises.answer: Yesterday I went to the park

homework.task: Write a diary entry (past tense) about yesterday and a plan (future tense) for the weekend.

revision.notes: Past: -ed (regular) or irregular. Present: base/add -s for he/she/it. Future: will + base form. Stay consistent!
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Writing: Paragraphs and Structure
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Write structured paragraphs with topic sentences
lessons.reading_material: A PARAGRAPH is a group of sentences about ONE idea. It starts with a TOPIC SENTENCE that states the main point. Then SUPPORTING SENTENCES give evidence, examples, or details. Finally, a CONCLUDING SENTENCE ties it up. CONNECTIVES link ideas: firstly, however, therefore, in addition, as a result, finally, in conclusion. Good writers PLAN before writing!
practical_activities: Paragraph sorting activity (mix up sentences)
Plan a persuasive paragraph
Peer edit for paragraph structure

exercises.q: The first sentence of a paragraph is often the?
Which connective shows cause? 'She was late, ___ she missed the bus.'

homework.task: Write 3 paragraphs about your favourite hobby. Include topic sentence, 3 details, conclusion sentence each.

revision.notes: Paragraph: topic sentence + 3-4 supporting sentences + concluding sentence. Plan: mind map or numbered list of points.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Classify natural resources as renewable or non-renewable
lessons.reading_material: Natural resources come from the Earth. Non-renewable resources (oil, coal, natural gas) take millions of years to form and will run out. Renewable resources (solar, wind, water, trees) can be replenished. Sustainable use means using resources without harming future generations.

Design a poster for energy conservation

homework.task: Track your family's energy use for one day — what could be reduced?

revision.notes: Renewable = can be replaced (sun, wind). Non-renewable = limited (coal, oil).

lessons.title: Earthquakes and Volcanoes
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Explain why earthquakes and volcanoes occur
lessons.reading_material: Earth's crust is divided into tectonic plates that move slowly. At plate boundaries, earthquakes and volcanoes occur. The 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific has many earthquakes and volcanoes. Richter scale measures earthquake strength.
practical_activities: Map the Ring of Fire
Simulate an earthquake with jelly and building blocks

lessons.title: Islamic Golden Age
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Identify key scholars and their contributions
lessons.reading_material: The Islamic Golden Age (8th–14th centuries CE) was a period of great learning centred in Baghdad (House of Wisdom). Scholars preserved and advanced Greek, Indian, and Persian knowledge. Key figures: Al-Khwarizmi (algebra), Ibn Sina/Avicenna (medicine), Al-Biruni (physics), Ibn Battuta (exploration). Advances in astronomy, optics, chemistry, and geography.
practical_activities: Research one Islamic scholar and create an info card
Trace the spread of Arabic numerals

homework.task: Find one word in English that comes from Arabic (e.g., algebra, chemistry, alcohol)

revision.notes: 8th–14th century: Baghdad = world centre of learning. Contributions to maths, medicine, science.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: The Mongol Empire
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Describe the rise of the Mongol Empire
Explain its impact on trade and cultures
lessons.reading_material: Genghis Khan united Mongol tribes around 1206 CE and created the largest contiguous empire in history. The empire stretched from China to Eastern Europe. It enabled Pax Mongolica: a period of stability that boosted Silk Road trade. But the Mongols also caused great destruction, including the sack of Baghdad in 1258.
practical_activities: Map the extent of the Mongol Empire
Debate: were the Mongols more destructive or beneficial?

homework.task: Research how the Mongol Empire affected trade along the Silk Road

revision.notes: Genghis Khan → largest land empire. Pax Mongolica = peace + trade. Destroyed Baghdad 1258.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Classic Children's Literature
lessons.subject: World Literature

lessons.reading_material: Classic children's literature has shaped generations of readers. 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' (Lewis Carroll, 1865) explores a curious girl's impossible journey. 'Arabian Nights / One Thousand and One Nights' (Arabic) collects tales from across the Middle East and Asia.
practical_activities: Book club discussion: compare one theme from 'The Little Prince' to a theme in 'Alice in Wonderland'
exercises: Who is the protagonist of 'The Little Prince'?

lessons.title: Fire Safety and Escape Plans
lessons.subject: Survival Skills
learning_objectives: Explain fire safety rules at home
Design a home fire escape plan
lessons.reading_material: Fires spread fast — you may have only 2 minutes to escape. Rules: never play with matches or lighters. Install smoke alarms on every floor. Have a home escape plan: know two ways out of every room, a meeting point outside (e.g. the big tree). If your clothes catch fire: Stop, Drop, Roll — stop moving, drop to the ground, cover your face and roll to put out flames. If there is smoke: crawl low where air is cleaner. Feel a door before opening — if hot, use another exit.
practical_activities: Design a home fire escape plan on graph paper — mark two exits from every room and a meeting point
exercises: Name 3 fire safety rules
What does 'Stop, Drop, Roll' mean?
Why should you crawl low in a smoky room?
lessons.homework: Walk through your home with a family member and identify all exits and smoke alarm locations.

revision.notes: Stop, Drop, Roll for burning clothes. Crawl low in smoke. Know 2 exits from every room.
revision.tip: Practise your escape plan with your family — real emergencies are not the time to learn it.

info_cards.fact: "Silent Spring" by Rachel Carson (1962) documented how the pesticide DDT was harming birds and wildlife, and is widely credited with leading to the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Abraham Lincoln
info_cards.fact: "Government of the people, by the people, for the people." — 16th president of the United States who led the country through the Civil War and helped end slavery.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: George Washington
info_cards.fact: "It is better to offer no excuse than a bad one." — American general and the first president of the United States, who led the colonies to independence from Britain.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Thomas Jefferson
info_cards.fact: "I cannot live without books." — Third U.S. president and principal author of the Declaration of Independence.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Benjamin Disraeli
info_cards.fact: "The secret of success in life is for a man to be ready for his opportunity when it comes." — British statesman who served as Prime Minister and was a prominent novelist.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Winston Churchill
info_cards.fact: "Success is not final, failure is not fatal: it is the courage to continue that counts." — British prime minister who led the United Kingdom through the Second World War.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Queen Elizabeth I
info_cards.fact: "I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman, but I have the heart and stomach of a king." — Queen of England whose long reign (1558-1603) is remembered as a golden age of English culture and exploration.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Queen Victoria
info_cards.fact: "We are not interested in the possibilities of defeat." — British monarch whose long reign saw vast industrial, cultural, and territorial growth of the British Empire.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Catherine the Great
info_cards.fact: "I praise loudly. I blame softly." — Empress of Russia who expanded the Russian Empire and championed arts and education.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Simon Bolivar
info_cards.fact: "A people that loves freedom will in the end be free." — South American military and political leader who helped lead several countries to independence from Spain.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Toussaint Louverture
info_cards.fact: "I want liberty and equality to reign throughout Saint-Domingue." — Leader of the Haitian Revolution who helped establish Haiti as the first Black-led republic.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Otto von Bismarck
info_cards.fact: "Politics is the art of the possible." — Prussian statesman who united the German states into the German Empire in 1871.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Theodore Roosevelt
info_cards.fact: "Do what you can, with what you have, where you are." — 26th U.S. president known for conservation efforts and progressive reforms.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Franklin D. Roosevelt
info_cards.fact: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself." — 32nd U.S. president who led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Eleanor Roosevelt
info_cards.fact: "No one can make you feel inferior without your consent." — American diplomat and activist who championed human rights and helped draft the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Nelson Mandela
info_cards.fact: "It always seems impossible until it's done." — South African leader who spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid and later became the country's first Black president.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Desmond Tutu
info_cards.fact: "Do your little bit of good where you are; it's those little bits of good put together that overwhelm the world." — South African archbishop and human-rights activist who fought against apartheid.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Wangari Maathai
info_cards.fact: "When we plant trees, we plant the seeds of peace and seeds of hope." — Kenyan environmental and political activist who founded the Green Belt Movement and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Aung San Suu Kyi
info_cards.fact: "Please use your freedom to promote ours." — Burmese politician and democracy advocate who spent years under house arrest for opposing military rule.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jawaharlal Nehru
info_cards.fact: "The light has gone out of our lives... yet the light that shone in this country was no ordinary light." — India's first prime minister who led the country in its early years of independence.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Indira Gandhi
info_cards.fact: "You cannot shake hands with a clenched fist." — India's first female prime minister who served for over fifteen years across two terms.

lessons.title: Measuring and Following a Recipe
lessons.subject: Cooking
learning_objectives: Read and follow a simple recipe
lessons.reading_material: A recipe gives instructions for making food. It lists ingredients (with amounts) and steps. Measuring accurately is important — too much flour makes bread heavy; too little sugar changes flavour. Kitchen measurements: grams (g), millilitres (ml), teaspoons (tsp), tablespoons (tbsp), cups. Cooking terms: fold (gently mix), whisk (beat with a fork or whisk), simmer (heat gently), dice (cut into small cubes), grate (scrape against a grater).
practical_activities: Make fruit salad following a given recipe — practise measuring each ingredient
exercises: Convert: 1 cup = how many ml (approx 240 ml)?
What does 'simmer' mean?
List 3 measuring tools used in cooking
lessons.homework: Find a simple recipe at home — list all ingredients and identify two cooking terms used.

revision.notes: Recipe = ingredients + steps. Key terms: fold, whisk, simmer, dice. Measure accurately.
revision.tip: Read the whole recipe before starting — surprises in step 8 ruin step 3.

quiz.question: Which tool measures liquid in ml?

lessons.assessment: Follow a provided recipe exactly and present your dish — scored on following instructions.

lessons.title: Government and Citizenship
lessons.subject: Social Studies
lessons.reading_material: Government is the system by which a country or community is controlled and organised. Governments make laws, provide services (schools, roads, hospitals), and maintain order. Citizens are members of a country with both rights (freedom of speech, education) and responsibilities (obeying laws, voting). Types of government include democracy (citizens vote for leaders), monarchy (a king or queen rules), and republic (elected government with no monarch). Most modern governments are democratic.
practical_activities: Classroom government: elect a class leader and discuss what rules they should make
exercises: What is the purpose of government?
Name two rights and two responsibilities of citizens
Explain the difference between a democracy and a monarchy
lessons.homework: Research the type of government in your country and name the current head of state.

revision.notes: Government makes laws and provides services. Citizens have rights and responsibilities.
revision.tip: In a democracy, the power comes from the people — YOU.

lessons.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
lessons.subject: Environmental Science
learning_objectives: Explain what happens when one species is removed
lessons.reading_material: Energy flows through ecosystems via food chains. Producers (plants) make food from sunlight. Primary consumers eat plants. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Decomposers break down dead matter. Remove one link and the whole chain is disrupted.
practical_activities: Build a local food web from given species cards
Simulate the effect of removing one species
exercises: Draw a food chain with 4 links
Predict the effect of removing rabbits from a grassland food web
lessons.homework: Research a keystone species and explain its role in its ecosystem.

revision.notes: Energy is lost at each link in the food chain — that's why there are always fewer predators than prey.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

options: A plant that makes food from sunlight
questions.correct: A plant that makes food from sunlight

questions.question: What happens if one species in a food web is removed?

questions.correct: The populations of linked species are affected

lessons.assessment: Draw a food web for your local environment with at least 8 species.

lessons.title: Introduction to Business
lessons.subject: Business Studies
lessons.reading_material: A business is an organisation that produces goods or provides services to satisfy the needs and wants of people. Businesses can be small (like a local bakery) or large (like a supermarket chain). Entrepreneurs are people who start and run businesses, taking risks in hopes of making a profit. Every business needs customers — the people who buy the goods or use the services.
practical_activities: Draw your own imaginary business — name it, decide what it sells, and design a logo
exercises: List 5 goods and 5 services you use at home
Give one example each of a small business and a large business
Why might someone choose to start their own business?
lessons.homework: Find a local business and write 3 sentences describing what it sells and who its customers are.

revision.notes: A business produces goods (things you can touch) or services (actions done for you). Entrepreneurs take risks to earn profit.
revision.tip: Think of a business you visit regularly — what need does it meet?

quiz.question: Which of these is a SERVICE?

lessons.assessment: Draw and label a simple business — name, product/service, target customers.
